Gavric: "When we talked about that, I first only passed information that in that area, according to our information, there was no one, and if you come across someone, bring him to us and report that to us. The people who are responsible for that, that they can have informative discussions with them whether there were any more Muslims in the area or not." I'm moving on to page 30. "But my question is when you met up with these units and you were explaining that they were explaining what was going to happen, did you pass on to them the comments of your commander?" "Yes, I did it right here, I did it right there." Question: "In Sandici, where you linked up? "That's where I presented that all to them. That is the area we were going to search where we believed there was no enemy soldiers, but if there was some left behind, they would have to report that to us and bring them to us so that we would have official information whether there was anybody or not." And finally, if we could go to page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This reading of transcript is improper. There's no impeachment, there's no refreshment of recollection, there's no point that I can see to it. This is taking another witness who is not here to be cross-examined... If there's a point, he can get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karnavas is going to finish the reading, so we are waiting for your question, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And let me read one other portion with respect to this issue, which is the issue of linking up with Mr. Gavric who was a Prosecution witness who was taken off the list just recently. Page 31, line 1, you'll find it on page 26 to 27 of the Serbian version. I read: "You told me earlier that when you were talking to your commander, you were going to the field to prevent any stupidity. First of all, what did that mean?" "It's human talk. We were aware that in a certain group of armed men, there are people who were consciously or not consciously willing or ready to do something stupid because in that, let's say, group there were probably people who lost son, or father or mother or brother or something, and they considered that their only opportunity to do something. And that's the reason I did it the way I did it. And that was the reason the commander told me what he did." Question: "And did the commander tell you to go in the field to stop that sort of stupidity or that was just understood?" "He told me to go and link them up. Those two units, in fact, those two commanders, because I knew them personally. And probably knowing me as a person, that if I go to carry out a certain task, it will be done properly, militarily." Now, my question is: According to Mr. Gavric, another Prosecution witness, he seems to indicate that he was not in command, he was not commanding you, he was not ordering you, but he was there merely to link you up with another unit of the Bratunac Brigade so you could coordinate the searching.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several units there. We were all on an assignment, an assignment that had been given to us, and that was to search the terrain from the start line, the start line I referred to yesterday in my testimony. So we coordinated units. The area had been unmowed during the war and it was hill-side. There had to be coordination and I carried out coordination as well as Captain Gavric. We were both carrying out our orders, orders given to us at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, the order to search the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. But we're talking about the issue of who was in command and whether you were resubordinated to the Bratunac Brigade and we seem to be getting some conflicting answers from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is never-ending. This is not a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we understand your point. I think you have done whatever you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on to another question, but in the same area, Your Honour. Hopefully...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it your understanding, sir, that in a situation such as this one where you're searching the terrain and you have MUP and military coordinating and working side by side, that this operation can only be done if there's resubordination of the MUP to the army? Is that your understanding of the rules?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Not a problem. In this situation, MUP was asked to participate in a searching of the terrain with other units, including the Bratunac Brigade. Is it your understanding under the rules that MUP could only assist in this sort of operation if it were to be resubordinated to the military?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP could assist the military and be resubordinated to the military. I don't think I understand your question sufficiently, to a sufficient degree. Can I have some clarification of that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, my question is: Does MUP necessarily have to be subordinated or can they coordinate and assist in a task while still maintaining their own command?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain to you that every sector of the terrain that was searched, I and Captain Gavric engaged the people, the line of the search, so that the people would not get separated, so that the personnel could carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And my question is: Is it your understanding that you had to be resubordinated to the Bratunac Brigade in order for you to carry out the searching operation or you could not participate at all?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we received our task at the Bratunac Brigade, we became resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Under what -- under what rule are you relying on?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On what basis did Mr. Borovcanin tell you, "I'm sending you to Bratunac. You're going to be resubordinated. You're going to be under their command. They will do what they please with you," as you seem to indicate the rules apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. It's not a serious question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a very serious question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's totally improper, then, Your Honour, if he's actually telling us he's serious. "Do as they please with you." This is nothing that has come out of this witness's mouth. This is Mr. Karnavas making argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As they may dispose of however they wish. I'll use his own term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we have been on this question for quite a long time and I don't think you could get more from the answer of this witness on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me turn to you -- to what another Prosecution witness has testified, at least with respect to this particular issue, and this was Mr. Obrenovic who testified after he had already made an agreement with the Prosecution to fully cooperate and testify truthfully, the implication being that there would be no motive for him to fabricate. And I want to show you a portion of his statement, the statement that was taken from him after he entered a plea, and for identification purposes is D52/1. I will be referring to page 110. Now, I just want to read for the record lines 10 to 22. This is a question by Peter McCloskey himself to Mr. Obrenovic when he gave his statement after he pled guilty, the statement being taken on 4 June, 2003: "Okay, the MUP were under the command of the army at this time. Is that right?" Answer: "On the 19th, I don't think that it was." Unintelligible. "We were conducting the sweeps separately. After the corridor was closed, each group was conducting its sweeps separately. Already on the 18th and further..." Unintelligible. "On the 22nd, there was a joint operation between the asphalt road and the general road in which combined units participated." Peter McCloskey, question: "It's hard for me to imagine the MUP working in the same woods that you are working in without being under the control of the army. That would be a very dangerous situation for both of you. Answer: "You are correct, but it was separate." Now, my question to you is this: Based on what Mr. Obrenovic has told the Prosecutor in a statement after he had admitted his guilt, would you agree or disagree with his interpretation, that is, that MUP can be searching side by side with an army unit and not necessarily be resubordinated to it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I can give you my statement in relation to what I did. As far as I can see, this is about events after the 18th. Already on the 19th, I had left this territory. So what was done later out in the field, I really don't know. His interpretation, I don't know how the units were operating out in the field in order for me to be able to interpret what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday I believe you indicated that there were about 200 men that were captured. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly about 200 surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was your testimony that they were turned over to Mr. Gavric and not to Stalin.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They surrendered to Mr. Gavric and to Mr. Stalin, whatever you wish. Then buses were requested. They were ordered on the buses. And they went in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, they were turned over to you, were they not, sir, except the children?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I know that we handed the children over to Captain Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you don't recall whether you took control over the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I can refer you to page 33 in the B/C/S -- in the Serbian version, and it's page 38 of Mr. Gavric's statement. And I'm referring to lines 5 and 6. He seems to indicate -- he states, being asked a question: "How many men and boys were in that group that you captured?" Page 33. I don't know the exact line. The question is: "How many men and boys were in that group that you captured?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GAVRIC STATES
utterances.text: "My free assessment, 35, 38." That's his assessment.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I stated to you and I'm stating before this Chamber that such and such a number of men surrendered and four children. And these four children were handed over to Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm not discussing the children, and I totally agree with you that the children were handed over to Mr. Gavric, who made it to their freedom thanks to Mr. Gavric. We're talking about his assessment of how many men were captured, and he indicates 35, 38, versus what you testified yesterday, which was approximately 200.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were about 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So he's either incorrect or you're incorrect, one of the two?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. I'm just telling you what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you don't remember whether these men that were captured were turned over to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that buses were requested. They boarded the buses and left in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let's see what Mr. Gavric has to say when he was being questioned by the Office of the Prosecution with the status of the witness. And I'm referring to page 16 and on your version it's page 14 of the Srpski version. And so for the English version, it's page 16. I'll be reading from lines 11 to 18 -- actually starting with line 10. Line 14, sir. I mean page 14. According to Mr. Gavric he states: "Just to make it short, that group of people that surrendered, that captured, I handed over to the people responsible to take them to Bijeljina. That's what I was told. They told me there was a camp somewhere around and they will be exchanged. I'll come to that moment. Some of them asked me, 'why are you doing it that way?' I said, 'I'm a soldier, that I respect the orders,' because my commander, every time he ordered me -- not me but to all was either a written or an oral order, in case you capture enemy soldiers, treat them according to the conventions. That was the order, and I follow that, I will always follow it. Now, I want to go to the next section, that's page 32 in the English version. That would be on page 27 to 28 of your version, sir, in Srpski. And I'll be reading from lines 3 and I'm going to be reading quite a bit. Okay. "And you said to me that you told them if they found someone to bring them back to you." "Yes, and that was done." Question: "Who is the appropriate people?" Referring to what he indicated two pages earlier. "So they were handed over to Jevic and his men, and I don't know where Jevic was stationed but they all went to Konjevic Polje." We don't have to read on but here he indicates that the men who were captured, prisoners, were handed over to you, sir. Now that we have seen this, does that refresh your memory at all as to whether the men were handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've already replied to that question. When those people surrendered and those four children appeared, buses arrived and they were all taken in the direction of Zvornik. I probably went to Konjevic Polje, stayed there for a brief period, and then came back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But here, a Prosecution witness who was on the list right before he got struck off, Mr. Gavric --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection for about the tenth time. He keeps making statements that are not part of the record, are not part of the question. It's completely inappropriate and uncalled for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: According to Mr. Gavric, he indicates to the Office of the Prosecution that he handed these prisoners to the appropriate authorities, and then he indicates that you were the appropriate authority, handed over to you personally. So my question is: Does this refresh your memory? Do you have a memory of the men being handed over to you and you being responsible for them?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've already replied to that question. I don't know what Mr. Gavric stated. I think that I am being very sincere. I have no reason to lie here. Buses were summoned. They arrived. The people boarded them and went in the direction of Zvornik. Four children were taken over by Captain Gavric and I don't know where he went with them. I don't know what happened to them afterwards. Anything else that I would tell you would be superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 39, and it's page 34 in your -- in the Serbian version. Page 39, I'm going to be reading from lines 20 to 22. Here Mr. Gavric again in answering a question to the Office of the Prosecution states that "From there they were handed over to Jevic and the rest of us just remained there waiting for the buses. They continued on foot with Jevic to Konjevic Polje." That's what Mr. Gavric told the OTP when he was interviewed as a witness back in November 28, 2001. Now, having heard what Mr. Gavric says here on page 39, lines 20 to 22, does this help your memory? Because he seems to be indicating here that he hands the men over to you and then he says that they continued on foot with Jevic to Konjevic Polje. So you're marching them, walking with them. You're doing something with them. Does this help trigger your memory?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as that is concerned, I've stated what I had to state clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go back -- let's go to page 40. And in your page it would be page 35. Lines 19 to 21. Mr. Gavric tells the Office of the Prosecution, "I told him that I returned to the field, that I brought the kids, that I handed over the man that I captured to the commander of the MUP unit. And he told me that I did good." This is where Mr. Gavric is reporting to someone back in the brigade what he did. So he reports that he handed the men over to you. Does this help your memory?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't understand. Okay. Let's go to page 41. It will be page 36. Lines 24, and I'm going to go on to page 42. Question: "And did he write down in the duty officer's book what you told this unknown officer?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GAVRIC
utterances.text: "He was pretty precise. I assume that we recorded somewhere. And for the children, I know for sure that they were filmed. Question: "Did you report the capture of the Muslims to anyone in the Bratunac Brigade?" "I had no reason to do so because I was not obliged to except for the duty officer." So when you come from the terrain, you're supposed to report to the duty officer and that man was sitting in the duty officer's room. Question: "And once you reported to the duty officer?" Answer: "I finished all my duty." Question: "And what would the duty officer do, report to the commander?" Answer: "Probably in his report." Now here, Mr. Gavric seems to indicate that he makes a record of the fact that he has the four children and he has turned over the men to you, the commander of MUP. Does this help refresh, rejuvenate, your memory somehow?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand you. I responded already. Mr. Gavric and myself were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But Mr. Gavric is very precise that the main --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is just going beyond -- this is about the tenth time that this has been asked and answered. It's unduly time-consuming and no longer very probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you have already answered your question and the witness answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my last question in that area, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We cannot get more from this witness, you have to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I just want to make sure the point is abundantly clear. Now that I think we are all clear, I am going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic, your commander, Mr. Borovcanin, has been indicted, has he not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, he was supposed to turn himself in, but he's on the run someplace. Right? Well, he's not in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's where he's supposed to be, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's been indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And you were at the time, the period that is covered in his indictment, you were the second in the command over the MUP units there, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were the next in line?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say that I was subordinated to him because there were a lot of police units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you were in Potocari on those critical days, the 12th and the 13th. Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your company commander, the person that you supervised and you ordered was also there, Mr. Djuric. Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And under the rules of subordination and the rules of chain of command, command responsibility, you would be responsible for any acts that he might have committed. Right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's your understanding. Is it fair to -- and I understand it that when you were questioned by the Prosecution and as you sit here today, you still remain a suspect, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I have been called here to testify. I stated when I was providing my first statement and when I talked with the Prosecutor here on Sunday, and I'm repeating it again here. My conscience as a human being and as an officer is clear. I have nothing to hide. Had I felt responsible in any sense, then of course I would -- I believe that I would need to be made accountable for that. This is what I stated in Banja Luka and this is what I am stating here now. Perhaps you view me as some kind of beast. You might feel that I committed some things, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As you sit here today, you remain a suspect by the Prosecution, not by the Defence. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot interpret the actions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that's why on the day of -- on the 12th of July, on the 13th of July, 1995, you saw no evil, you heard no evil, and now you're here to speak no evil. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I stated what I had heard. I cannot say anything about what was presented in the media or what was seen. I was never a supporter of that, but I cannot say that I saw what I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of today's and yesterday's testimony by Mr. Jevic and according to instructions from my client, I don't have any significant questions. I just wanted to put three or four relevant questions referring to the status of my client, but we can probably finish that before the break. May I be allowed to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may move on. We still have three minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Jevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to put a few questions to you. Do you personally know Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally hear about all the events that you participated in in Srebrenica, Bratunac, did you ever hear the name of Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you an athlete?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is your field?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judo. I was in competitions for a long time, and at the moment I'm a judo trainer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever play on the national team?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come to Zvornik because of that?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In all of your sports activities did you ever hear of a Lieutenant Dragan Jokic and any of the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of his name in connection with any events in Srebrenica. Had I heard that, I would have said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You are very efficient. You have finished your cross-examination in two minutes. Well, it is time for a break. We resume at 12.30. --- Break taken at 11.59 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-direct examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just a few minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic, regarding discipline, did you discipline any of your troops for abusing Muslims in any way, for their conduct from 11 July through the point where you went back to Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no reason to any disciplinary measures. As for my unit, the unit of which I was in command, according to the information I had, they did not abuse anyone or do any harm to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any investigation that you're aware of that your units were involved in any abuse of Muslim prisoners during that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any investigation by any government body of Ministry of the Interior troops in the Bratunac, Srebrenica, Konjevic Polje area during that time period?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None that I was aware of. Recently, the government carried out certain obligations pursuant to the human rights centre, and there was indeed an investigation into those things that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that ongoing today as we speak?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the government completed and submitted one of the reports now. Whether this is still ongoing, believe me, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you received your orders on the 17th at the Bratunac Brigade command, did you receive those orders from MUP or army?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received orders from the army. I was ordered by my superior, Borovcanin, to go to the meeting for an agreement concerning the assignment and the search of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you say you received orders at that meeting on the 17th from the army. Can you tell us who in the army you received the orders from?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember who was at the meeting. Activities were agreed at the meeting as to how the forces should be deployed during the search. My order to go to the meeting came from my superior, Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know the rank of the army individuals that gave you the orders at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- if it was main staff, corps, or brigade level army officers that gave you your orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. Excuse me, sir. Now it's multiple choice time. The Prosecutor got his answer, he got it repeatedly. Now he's giving him a multiple choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, I believe the witness has answered the question. You cannot get more from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, he has not been asked what division of the army he may have heard that from, be it the main staff, the corps or the brigade level. Those are the only thee choices. I can ask him if he knows what level. He might. The way things are going, I agree with you, he probably doesn't. It has not been asked and I thought it should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what level of army provided you those orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume the chain of command says that the main staff sends the order to the corps, the corps to the brigade, and the brigade to its units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know which of the three actually gave you the order?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the MUP have anything to do with the buses that the 200 prisoners were transported on on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know who was controlling the buses?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the MUP was in no position to control those buses. It could either have been the army or the civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you working with any civilian authority in this terrain operation, of sweeping the terrain?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any civilian authority that was involved in the transportation of the Muslim prisoners that day?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think happened to those 200 Muslim prisoners??

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation. He can ask him if he knows, and if so get the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could rephrase your question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were taken in the direction of Zvornik. Now, as for what happened later on, many things were being said in the media, but whether that was precisely what happened to that specific group of prisoners, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any information about what the children were reporting to the army and the MUP after they were captured?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. It's beyond the scope of cross-examination at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, the children you mentioned, is that four children, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think this question is beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, he's asking what the children said with respect to what they saw, as opposed to what they saw prior to them being captured. In my opinion, and I don't want to disagree with the Trial Chamber, in my opinion it is beyond the scope. I'm not afraid of the answer, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But this question is somewhat relevant to the issue. It's related to this issue and of course hearsay evidence, there's no problem for us to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But Mr. Karnavas, and if you believe this is beyond the scope, you still have the right to pursue on this subject later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's precisely why I registered my concern, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic, did you -- I'll try to ask the question again. Did you receive any information about what the children that were captured were reporting after their capture?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to just briefly go back to this exhibit, Your Honour, I think you mentioned, P159, this report that has Mr. Borovcanin's name on the back of it. If I could show that to the witness one more time and try to clarify some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jevic, this document begins by saying: "By order number 64/95 issued by the deputy minister of the interior on 10 July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honour, the 10 July order, which was Exhibit P157A does, in fact, say that it's order 64/95.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a report like this that's drafted in this particular style of numbered paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have seen Mr. Borovcanin; he's written several reports on the various combat activities that he was involved in. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And has he showed you many of the reports of combat activities that he's written to the minister involving these sorts of things?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You haven't seen his reports? I'm not talking about this incident. I'm talking about just regular combat reports that he sends to Mr. Kovac. Have you seen any of his normal reports that he would write like from Trnovo or Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In any report that Mr. Borovcanin would make, is it -- should there be something on the front page of it or was it normal to start out like this with no heading or no date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's a lack of foundation here and, you know, I think he needs to ask a few questions before he can get to that. And also might I remind everyone that this is the Prosecution's exhibit. So now it appears that he's impeaching his own witness with this exhibit. So I just -- I don't understand the line of questioning that he's getting into. Does he want the witness to acknowledge that this is an official document or that it was fabricated? Because, after all, this was brought here by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the Prosecutor asked a proper question, because this is a question we want to ask at a later stage. I look forward to your cooperation and let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try again. Is it normal for this to start out like this without some sort of a cover page?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The established procedure for drafting the rules would be to have the header in the upper left corner, stating the name of the institution, of the republic and of the state; the institution, the seat of the institution, then perhaps additional signs, symbols, the document number, and then the date. Below that, there would be a description of the procedure, or rather the document being submitted, whether it was notes, minutes, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and how about the -- could you put the front page of your B/C/S version on the ELMO. Just the front page, just so we can take a -- so people can see what that looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, we have some problems with the LiveNote. So would you please pause for a while, we could have some technicians to look into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. McCloskey, would you please try again. It seems to me that the LiveNote is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We have this document on the ELMO so we can see the front of it. Would this be a normal beginning of an official document?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've just told us that normally there would be a heading and a date on it. There's not a heading and a date on this anywhere, is there?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was speaking about the text itself. As for the heading and date, that would be in the upper left corner, typed in the upper left corner. The name of the state, country, the name of the institution, the place where the institution is located, then you would have the date and then the type of the document specified, a report or something like that. At first I didn't understand your question, but now I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this particular page in and of itself, you don't see anything wrong with it. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no heading. There's no document number. There's no date and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There may be another page that's supposed to go with this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be another page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last page. Could you turn to the last page of this document. And maybe the usher will help you get it just so we can see. First of all, before we get to that, can you tell us what is normally on the last page of any official document such as a report like this?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The established procedure would be to have the person submitting the report there and to have the recording clerk there as well as the stamp of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this is the last page we have. Now, I'm not asking about the content of what's there, but should there be something else? If this was truly the last page, should those other things you mentioned be on there?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the bottom right corner, a bit under the text there should be the name of the person who submits the report typed up and signed and a stamp, a stamp endorsing the document, the stamp of the institution submitting the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there a difference between the original report that is written, signed, and stamped, and the same report that is received at the other end of a Teletype machine? Do they look differently?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean do they look different? Well, this report which arrived by fax or by telex, how should I explain this? I can't quite find the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can ask you something in particular. When a military document is encoded and teletyped over the airwaves, does the actual handwritten signature of the person that signed it go through the Teletype machine?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It works differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- so you do have some knowledge about what documents look like that go through the Teletype versus the ones that are originally signed?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From that little knowledge, can you take a look at this document in front of you and tell us whether you can tell if this was teletyped or might be not something that was sent over Teletype?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this document may have gone through a fax and was copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it possible to encrypt faxes at the time in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of last questions about -- this name down at the bottom, I'm just not -- can you clarify for us. You have seen Mr. Borovcanin's signature many times, as you've testified before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, having seen that signature before, what can you tell us about the way this name is written? And you can take another look at it. It's right there.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I understand, this does not entirely resemble his signature. His signature is, in fact, quite different. I did say this morning in relation to that, that wasn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Jevic, can you tell us what was your position and rank in special police brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for operations and training with the special brigade of the police. And my rank was lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: During the proofing at the ICTY premises on 19th October this year, you stated that Borovcanin was a colonel and held the equivalent position in the MUP as Krstic held in the army, and that's why Krstic, not Blagojevic would communicate orders to Borovcanin. To what army rank, your rank, in the police force was equivalent in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are different interpretations that are possible in this case. Borovcanin was not Mr. Krstic's equal in terms of rank. But establishment-wise and because of the units that he had command over at that time, he did have the level required to talk directly to General Krstic. The equivalent to my rank, well at the time it might have been the equivalent on my rank, rather, that I could command a detachment or something like that. That would have been my level roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Who would communicate orders to you? Who would give orders to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My commander was Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: General Krstic could give orders to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean me personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to communicate directly with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: During the proofings, you stated that on 10th July, 1995, you received a written order signed by Tomislav Kovac to report to the Bratunac Brigade. Then you reported to the Bratunac headquarters on 11th July, 1995, at 1500 hours. Whom did you report to?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not report to the command of the Bratunac Brigade, but I reported to Mr. Borovcanin in Bratunac. On the 11th at 1500 hours when I arrived at Bratunac, I reported to Mr. Borovcanin, my superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: As far as I understand, because Mr. Borovcanin didn't belong to Bratunac Brigade, you were ordered to report to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If you are talking about the 17th -- are you talking about the 17th or the 11th. I'm sorry. Which date are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: 11th, July 11th.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ordered to go to Bratunac and to wait there, that I would get an order from Mr. Borovcanin there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you ever received orders from Captain Nikolic or Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already stated, Your Honour, that I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You stated that on the 16th of July, 1995, you have met with Momir Nikolic at Bratunac Brigade to discuss the search operation. Can you tell us the details of your discussion.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was conveyed an order to report to the Bratunac Brigade to Mr. Nikolic and that I would be told when there would be a meeting which would deal with the next day's activities. I reported at 2300 hours and I was told that the meeting would be between 7.00 and 8.00 a.m. in the morning at the command of the Bratunac Brigade. I don't remember exactly the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What issues did you discuss at this meeting with Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a meeting. I just reported to him so that I would get the time for the meeting and to see what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judge's questions? Yes, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that there's no questions. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I might be able to clarify one point for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, it says on the arrival - of this 10 July order - on arrival at the destination, the unit commander shall contact General Krstic. Who do you believe that unit commander to have been, according to this order?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All items of that order need to be looked at in order to understand who was to contact General Krstic. One of the items allocates Mr. Borovcanin as the superior of all the police forces and as the only person to be able to contact General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. P157, the 10 July order under the name of Mr. Kovac I would tender. And as regarding P159, the report with Mr. Borovcanin's name on it, if I could have a short discussion outside the presence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We -- there's a possibility that we could revisit this issue at a later stage. Any objections as for the document P157?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. We were going to be asking that -- urging the Prosecution to admit it. So we're glad to see that they're doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections to admitting these two documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The document P157 is admitted into the evidence. And later on we will discuss about that document P159. Are there any documents that Defence team would like to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. D60/1, the Official Gazette of the Serbian people of -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina, defence act, that's the law on defence; D61/1, the law on the implementation of the law on internal affairs during an imminent threat of war or a state of war; D62/1, which is the Republika Srpska President of the Republika Srpska order. And we would encourage the Prosecution to think about admitting their P109 which was the CJB document that we made reference to, and that is dated July 13th, 1995, where it shows that Mr. Vasic clearly indicates that based on the meeting from General Mladic that the MUP have been yielded to do certain tasks, and we think that's a vital piece of evidence. It now carries for identification purposes P109. So we would ask that that be admitted as well, but at this point in time it is a Prosecution evidence, but we are willing to adopt it and put our own number on it. We hesitate because we don't want to cloud up or confuse the system. But we welcome every opportunity to use the Prosecution evidence whenever we can, and introduce them as Defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, no to the first group. As for P109, this is an issue we've crossed before. This is an important document. It comes within a series of documents on similar dates and should best be seen in context with all those documents -- and we don't have a foundation for it yet. So I would prefer that we wait until we have a foundation for it. But if the Court wants it in evidence now, I can certainly tell you we will provide an authentic and accurate foundation as much as possible for this document, as it was obtained in a search warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you have no objections to other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. The others, those are all part of Mr. Butler's report, and were all, most of them anyway, and we agree that those -- and those are more along the lines of rules and regulations, more in line of public-oriented type documents, so I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the document tendered by Defence team, D60, D61, and D62 are admitted into evidence. As for the document P109, I believe that the Defence team would like to tender it into the evidence as his evidence. Since this document is provided by the OTP and we would make a tentative decision that to admit this document into the evidence at this stage, and since it's tendered by Defence, maybe we could have a Defence number on it. Of course, there's still room for further informations and further cooperations on this piece of document at a later stage. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, thank you, Your Honour. Secondly, we don't want to take ownership, we just want to make sure it gets into the evidence, whether it's P109 or D64, it's fine with us. If we are to give it a number, then I believe the next number would be D64/1. And I'm perfectly willing to allow the Prosecution the time that is necessary to introduce it when they believe it's -- so I'm not -- as long as I have a good faith representation that they're going to be introducing it, I have no problem in waiting. We did use the document. So, again, I don't want confuse the numbering system, but I leave it up to the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is a tentative ruling on this piece of document. And I think it is tendered by Defence, at this moment we will have a Defence number on it. To me, there's no difference whether the ownership is yours or the Prosecution's. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you have a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, how about that document P159.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That document was provided to us by Mr. Vasic, and it was in the format that you have seen it, apparently missing a top page and a bottom page. I don't find that to be a very reliable source of information, though it's an interesting document. And I'm reluctant at this time to offer a document like this that could be fabricated into evidence, though I say it's an interesting document to compare and I know Your Honours will give it the weight that you feel it's appropriate based on that. We would like to do a little more work to see if there's any way we can try to authenticate it any further and hopefully I can provide the Court with some more information on that. But, again, I have no objection if the Court feels it's something they want to consider. But I would like to be able, before offering it into evidence, provide you with a little more substance on whether it's authentic or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas, what's your view on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I'm somewhat lost for words. A rare occasion, but nonetheless we have it. Why if they have a problem with the authenticity of the document would they even bring it in? I don't know. I concur with the Prosecutor that it lacks the necessary foundation, but why even bother to bring it in only to then suggest that it shouldn't be brought in. That's why I was a little confused because it seemed like yesterday they wanted it in and today they want to impeach it. So, I don't know what to think of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's something out of scope of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know. I understand that. What I want to know is your view with this document, whether it should be admitted into the evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Stojanovic, your colleague, has agreed that this document could be admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour, to it being admitted into evidence. I would agree with the Prosecutor that there may be some problems, however I have no objections. I do think it's something that the Court should consider. And in fact, I would welcome the opportunity. I sincerely say this, for the Prosecution to bring Mr. Vasic here, subpoena him, bring him here, so we can question him, because it's Mr. Vasic who provided them with the letter with respect to what Mr. Kovac saw when Mladic ordered on the 13th, made the famous "kill them all," statement and as a result the events were put into motion, which is what we believe happened. I don't have any objections and I would urge the Prosecutor on the record, since they do have some concerns about the foundation to bring Mr. Vasic, and maybe Mr. Vasic could assist us all in laying a better foundation. I have no objections to it and I think the Court can consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I respond to Mr. Karnavas. He's insinuated that there's something improper about my bringing this document in and I would like to just be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have a witness waiting from 9.00 this morning and it's quite a long time, at least we have to hear parts of his testimony this morning. Let us not debate that. I think I'm in a position to make ruling concerning the document. Since the Defence team do not object to the admission of this document, we would like to make a ruling that this document P159 is admitted into the evidence. But however, unless the Prosecution will provide us with more information concerning of the authenticity of this document, we'll attach very little weight on this document. It is so decided. Well, I think we should hear the next witness. Good morning, Ms. Davis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I wanted to inform the Court this witness has decided to testify in open session. I believe you all have been informed of that already, but I wanted to say on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness -- or good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. And before you start, I think I have to warn you that you may object to making any statement which might intend to incriminate yourself. But however, the Chamber may compel you to answer the question. Testimonies compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against you for any offense, other than the false testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Davis, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Do you remember meeting with me and an investigator and also an interpreter was present in our offices on Monday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Were you told at that time that you had a right to have an attorney present with you and that you had a right to remain silent?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And you waived those rights at that time and you agreed to talk with us. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And you also agreed to testify in court here today without the assistance of counsel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Would you please state for the record your name and spell your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: N-i-k-o-l-a G-a-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what is your birth date, Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: January 1st, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that for the interpreter, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Opravdici--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like to make a correction to the birth date. It was January 5th, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, during the war, did you serve in the VRS during the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And when did you begin your service in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: 1992, in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And which unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: The Kravica Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: What brigade was the Kravica Battalion a part of?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the battalion -- the Kravica Battalion commander was in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Lazar Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And where was the battalion based?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: In the area of the Magasici village.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Were you also a member of a platoon or a company within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The intervention platoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what was your rank when you began service in the VRS in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I was lance corporal. I had that rank already from the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And in 1995 what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing. It was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And you were also in the intervention platoon of the Kravica Battalion in 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention to July 11th, 1995, the day that Srebrenica fell, and ask you where you and your platoon were positioned on that day.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: In the area of the Magasici village, that's where our line was.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: When you say "that's where our line was," can you describe to me what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Our line of defence was facing the Muslim forces in the village of Cizmici. That's where we were, between the village of Cizmici and the village of Magasici.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what were your orders and responsibilities with respect to the line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: We were there reinforcing the line for the eventuality of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: What could you see from your position in terms of combat activity or -- from your vantage point on the defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: There were no combat operations. You could see the UN checkpoint, the UNPROFOR checkpoint, and the Muslim villages that lay ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I understand you were there with your platoon members on the defence line, were there other units there as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing, the army that was always there, our army from the battalion. We were merely reinforcing them. We were reinforcing some of the trenches there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: You were reinforcing other units from your battalion?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. The company that was already there in the area, we reinforced them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: So was this area in Magasici and Cizmici, the area that you described, that was the area that was normally patrolled by your unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hate to object. Now she's indicating he was patrolling. It seems a fact not in evidence. He indicated that he was there. The lines were there. There was no such thing about patrolling. I would ask that the Prosecutor be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Davis, be careful with the terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. Mr. Karnavas is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Was this an area to which your unit was ordinarily assigned?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to a map that I'm going to place on the ELMO. This is marked for identification as exhibit P162. I would ask the usher to place it on the ELMO. We discussed earlier, Mr. Gajic, that we met briefly in our offices on Monday. And you might remember that I asked you to mark several locations on this map. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: One of the things that I asked you to mark was the approximate location of the defence line that you've described. And if you could, using one of the pens on your desk there, point to the line that you marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: It was something like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what were the end points approximately of the line that you marked on the map, in other words, the end points of the defence line that your unit was responsible for reinforcing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you mean the intervention platoon only or the whole battalion?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: If you can explain to us the end points of the defence line that your battalion was responsible for reinforcing.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. From about here from the village of Hranca towards Mount Ravni Buljin in the area of the village of Slikovici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I apologise. With respect to the markings that you made on the map. I see on the map a letter A that is next to the defence line. Did you make that marking?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the answer. May the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The interpreter is having some difficulty hear you, perhaps you could speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And that marks the eastern end of the line that you marked on the map. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the specific date of July 11th, the date that Srebrenica fell, what was occurring in the area where you were stationed along the defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing special, meaning we were just reinforcing the line and we were on duty there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Did you see any combat activity?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Not where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Did you -- could you, from your vantage point along the line, see anything in areas that you weren't reinforcing along the line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: From where I was, the only thing I could see was the UN checkpoint and the village of Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: So on the 11th of July, you were stationed along the defensive line and there was nothing that your unit was doing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time of whether there was any activity elsewhere along the defence line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have a clarification, what's defence line? Because the testimony will bear out throughout the trial that the Bratunac Brigade had a defence line throughout the period of way -- the time it was established all the way past the events of Srebrenica, and that was considered the defence line. So if we could have some clarification. His defence line, where he was situated? Somewhere further down the road, some foundation may need to be laid, if he's going to be asked to comment about other areas which he was not in sight of at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we might spend some time on that issue. Ms. Davis, you may ask some questions in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, from where you were positioned on the defence line, how far -- and you may indicate on the map, how far to the west could you see?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking as far as Ravne Buljin mount.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And how far to the east could you see from where you were on the defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, not very far, due to the lie of the land, maybe as far as the next village in those hills.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Can you indicate using the pointer, the pen that you have in your hand, where the area of Ravni Buljin is.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Ravni Buljin, this area here, this smaller mountain, Rogac, it was near the mountain of Rogac, the village of Lipenovici. It was in that area. It was not a mountain. A hill perhaps would be a more fitting description.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: From where you were located on the defence line, being able to see over to Ravni Buljin, what if anything did you see on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember if it was the 11th of July, but one could see columns of people moving, the Muslims were coming out in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: You said "the Muslims were coming out." From what direction were the Muslims coming out?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: From the Srebrenica area on to Zvornik and Tuzla, in that general direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I take it from your previous answers that there were no Muslims coming out of Srebrenica in the direction of your position on the defence line. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Did you or did your platoon have any orders with respect to what you should do if any Muslims did attempt to come out of Srebrenica in your area of the defence line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, those who were not putting up resistance should be taken to the command posts, should any happen to be in the area, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: When you say "should any happen to be in the area," do you mean any Muslims happen to be in the area or any command posts. I didn't understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And when you say that they should be taken to the command post, what do you mean by the command post?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean the command of our battalion. What they would then do, I really don't know. Whether they would then send them on somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Do you believe that they had orders to send them on somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Davis, it is speculation. You may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether they have orders to send them on anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such order.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The night of -- the night that Srebrenica fell, the 11th of July, overnight until the 12th, can you tell me where you spent that night.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the same as before, our line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what happened on the 12th of July, the day after Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I'm not sure about the dates, but I know that the next time we moved it was as far as the UN checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And where was the UN checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: It was past the village of Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Looking again at exhibit P162 on the map that's on the ELMO there, do you remember marking on the map yesterday -- excuse me, on Monday, the location of Cizmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Can you point using the pen in your hand to the location on the map and indicate which letter is written by the village of Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: The letter C.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: You indicated that you moved as far as the UN checkpoint at Cizmici. When you say you moved, who moved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the military who were there in the area, the intervention platoon, and the remaining soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: So the members of your platoon moved?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Did the whole defence line move?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Defence line covers the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd and the 4th battalions. There's no foundation laid that this gentleman would know that information. If the foundation can be laid, that's fine. But when he's talking about the defence line, we have to remember, it's a long line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a reasonable objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: The defence line in your area where your platoon was stationed, did that portion of the defence line move south towards the village of Cizmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: One section, the intervention platoon and a small number of other soldiers moved along with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what did you find when you arrived in the village of Cizmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing. When we arrived, the village was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Were there any people there in the village at all when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement in June of 2002 to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Do you recall telling the investigator with whom you were speaking that you encountered UN soldiers when you arrived in the village of Cizmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes. But as I said a minute ago, the checkpoint was just outside the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I apologise. Was the checkpoint -- did you arrive at the checkpoint before you arrived at the village or after?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you -- was the checkpoint first or the village first from the direction you were coming?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: First the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: We met UN soldiers there. We spent some time there. We exchanged uniforms, things like that. Nothing special, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: When you said that you exchanged uniforms, do you mean that you gave them some uniforms and they gave you some uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: What did they give you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. We traded boots, jackets, shirts, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And so I take it they also -- you also gave them something?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Depends on who you're talking about. I, for one, gave them my boots.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: So was this a friendly exchange?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Friendly, what else? No debate going on, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Well, did they give you equipment voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: And what did the UN soldiers do after this exchange of equipment?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how long they stayed, but later they returned to their base in Potocari. That's to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Well, you say you're not sure how long they stayed. Can you estimate how long they stayed after you arrived in the UN checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA GAJIC
utterances.text: It may have been between one and three hours, one, two, three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to break here. It might be a good spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's stop at that Cizmici village today. Well, witness, I'm afraid that you have to spend another day in The Hague. And I have to remind you that while you're in The Hague, you're still under the oath, so do not let anybody talk to you and do not talk to anybody about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of October, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
